abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), significant progress has been made in multi-agent applications. However, the complexities in coordinating agents’ cooperation and LLMs’ erratic performance pose notable challenges in developing robust and efficient multi-agent applications. To tackle these challenges, we propose AgentScope, a developer-centric multi-agent platform with message exchange as its core communication mechanism. The abundant syntactic tools, built-in agents and service functions, user-friendly interfaces for application demonstration and utility monitor, zero-code programming workstation, and automatic prompt tuning mechanism significantly lower the barriers to both development and deployment. Towards robust and flexible multi-agent application, AgentScope provides both built-in and customizable fault tolerance mechanisms. At the same time, it is also armed with system-level support for managing and utilizing multi-modal data, tools, and external knowledge. Additionally, we design an actor-based distribution framework, enabling easy conversion between local and distributed deployments and automatic parallel optimization without extra effort. With these features, AgentScope empowers developers to build applications that fully realize the potential of intelligent agents. We have released AgentScope at https://github.com/modelscope/agentscope, and hope AgentScope invites wider participation and innovation in this fast-moving field.

sections.body: The introduction lists three development challenges: specialized agent configurations, SOP or dynamic workflows, and varied communication patterns. It also names LLM hallucination and unreliable instruction-following as sources of errors that can cascade through a system. Multi-modal data, tools, retrieval-augmented generation, and distributed deployment are named as further requirements. The section states the platform's goals as usability, robustness, and efficiency. It reports no experiments; the claims are design claims supported by the feature descriptions in later sections.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Multi-agent application development is hard, so the paper proposes AgentScope, a platform built around message exchange.

sections.body: Messages are Python dictionaries with mandatory name and content fields and an optional url field. Agents expose reply and observe functions. Workflows are sequences of agent executions and message exchanges. Service functions return a ServiceResponse, and tools are service functions with descriptions and pre-filled parameters. The architecture has a utility layer, a manager and wrapper layer, and an agent layer, plus user interfaces including a terminal, a Web UI monitor, and a Gradio interface. The section is descriptive and reports no quantitative evaluation.
sections.heading: Overview
sections.headline: AgentScope defines four core concepts (message, agent, service, workflow) and a three-layer architecture.

sections.body: Pipelines encapsulate sequential, conditional, and iterative message exchange. The message hub broadcasts messages to a group of agents. Table 1 lists built-in agents such as DialogAgent, ReActAgent, and ProgrammerAgent. Automatic prompt tuning generates system prompts from a short agent description, and an in-context learning switch selects demonstrations by random selection, similar questions, or similar answers. The workstation generates JSON configuration or Python code from dragged modules. The section gives no user study or timing measurements to show that these features lower development effort.
sections.heading: High Usability
sections.headline: Pipelines, a message hub, built-in agents, and a drag-and-drop workstation are offered to reduce development effort.

sections.body: The four error levels are accessibility errors, rule-resolvable errors, model-resolvable errors, and unresolvable errors. Retry logic is provided for accessibility errors, with a configurable maximum retry count. Rule-based correction repairs issues such as unmatched braces without another LLM call. Developers can supply `parse_func`, `fault_handler`, and `max_retries` for custom handling. A logging system with a CHAT level is the last safeguard. The section describes these mechanisms but reports no measurements of how often they recover from errors.
sections.heading: Fault-Tolerant Mechanisms
sections.headline: Errors are sorted into four levels, each handled by retries, rule-based correction, customizable handlers, or logging.

sections.body: Multi-modal data is stored locally through a file manager, and model wrappers return a local URL after saving generated content. Messages carry the URL, so the data is loaded on demand when rendered in the web UI or passed to a model wrapper. The paper states three benefits: smaller messages, the possibility of parallel text and multi-modal processing, and easier demonstration in interfaces. Named models include DALL-E and GPT-4V. The section gives no latency or throughput figures to measure these benefits.
sections.heading: Multi-Modal Applications
sections.headline: Multi-modal data is passed as URLs in messages, with files loaded only when needed.

sections.body: Developers register service functions with preset arguments, and the toolkit generates JSON schema descriptions. During iterative reasoning, the LLM returns a JSON dictionary in a fenced code block with thought, speak, and function fields. During acting, the toolkit parses the response and executes the function. Parsing and execution errors are returned to the LLM for correction, while other runtime errors go to the developer. Parsers exist for fenced code blocks, JSON objects, and tagged content. The section does not evaluate tool-use accuracy.
sections.heading: Tool Usage
sections.headline: The service toolkit implements a ReAct loop with four steps: function preparation, instructions, reasoning, and acting.

sections.body: A single .json file groups RAG configuration, covering document directories, file types, segmentation tools, and indexing models. Knowledge banks hold RAG objects with unique `knowledge_id` values, so agents can share indexes instead of rebuilding them. An RAG agent can load several RAG objects, insert, delete, or replace knowledge at runtime, and weight results from different objects. The section states that compatibility with LlamaIndex and LangChain is intended. It includes no retrieval quality measurements.
sections.heading: Agents with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.headline: Retrieval-augmented generation support uses a one-file configuration and shared knowledge banks that agents can update and weight.

sections.body: Agents run as actors that compute once their input messages are ready, which yields automatic parallel execution without a static graph. Placeholder messages let the main process continue without blocking, and the process blocks only when a placeholder is used in control flow. Agent servers can be started on remote machines, and AgentScope Studio gathers messages from distributed agents. Examples 14 to 16 show converting a local workflow with `to_dist` and changing only the agent configuration. The section states that efficiency is demonstrated but reports no benchmark numbers.
sections.heading: Actor-based Distributed Framework
sections.headline: An actor-based distributed mode lets the same workflow run locally or across machines, using placeholder messages.

sections.body: The werewolf game is implemented in about one hundred lines of code with six players in two teams. Group conversation uses the message hub and an `@agent_name` mention feature. The copilot uses LlamaIndex-based RAG agents, and the web search example runs SearcherAgent and AnswererAgent. The natural language to SQL example uses a ReAct agent with DAIL-SQL prompts over an SQLite database. Local and distributed deployments are shown for the basic conversation example. The section presents these as demonstrations and reports no task success rates.
sections.heading: Signature Applications of AgentScope
sections.headline: Example applications include basic and group conversation, a six-player werewolf game, a retrieval-augmented generation copilot, web search, and a database query agent.

sections.body: The section describes language agent frameworks including the Transformers library, LangChain, AutoGPT, and ModelScope-Agent. It describes multi-agent frameworks including AutoGen, MetaGPT, AGENTS, OpenAgents, ChatDev, CAMEL, and AgentSims. For each, it summarizes the framework's stated focus, such as SOP encoding in MetaGPT or role-playing in CAMEL. The section positions AgentScope around ease of use, fault tolerance, and versatility. It makes no quantitative comparison with these systems.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Related frameworks such as LangChain, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev are grouped into language agent and multi-agent frameworks.

sections.body: The conclusion states that AgentScope offers communication and distributed mechanisms, fault-tolerant operation, and multi-modal interaction. It says the platform abstracts complexity and provides development utilities. Future work is named as deeper RAG integration, adaptive communication protocols, and interactive modalities. The conclusion also states predicted industrial impact in healthcare and customer service. These are stated expectations; the paper provides no measured evidence for them in the text given.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that AgentScope lowers barriers to multi-agent development and lists RAG and adaptive protocols as future work.

sections.body: Appendix A shows the dialog history of a standalone conversation in Listing 22. Appendix B refers to the complete werewolf code in the AgentScope GitHub repository and provides an example dialogue history in Listing 23. The appendix contains no new method details or evaluation results. Its content is supporting material for the example applications in the preceding section.
sections.heading: Appendix
